title: Hubble view of NGC 2366
caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 2366, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2363, NGC 2366 · constellation Camelopardalis · about 10 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the dwarf galaxy NGC 2366 in detail. It has none of the elegant spiral arms seen in many larger galaxies, but it does hold a bright nebula where stars are forming.

The galaxy is also close enough that astronomers can make out its individual stars. That is valuable, because studying single stars in another galaxy lets researchers compare them directly with the stars of our own. In more distant galaxies, the light of countless stars blends together into a smooth glow.

Dwarf galaxies are much smaller than galaxies like the Milky Way, and many lack a tidy shape. A star-forming nebula is a cloud of gas lit up by hot young stars born inside it. In NGC 2366, that nebula stands out as a bright region among the galaxy's scattered stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.22 x 1.96 arcminutes) and distance (10 million light years), the frame spans roughly 15,000 × 5,700 light-years. Its light set out about 10 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy's individual stars are far too faint to see by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: NGC 2366 lies about 10 million light-years away in the constellation Camelopardalis. ESA's entry for this image also lists the object NGC 2363.
alt: A dwarf galaxy made of many individual stars with a bright star-forming nebula.
